title: Microscopic theory of the lower critical field in superconducting thin-film strips
abstract: The lower critical field \(B_{c1}\) of a narrow superconducting thin-film strip sets the thermodynamic scale for vortex-free operation in a perpendicular magnetic field. The standard Pearl--London estimate requires a phenomenological vortex-core cutoff, because the London theory does not resolve the core. We formulate a microscopic theory for a dirty strip by solving the two-dimensional Usadel equations in the film plane, with the applied field included directly in the gauge-invariant momentum. Self-consistent vortex and Meissner solutions are computed at fixed field, and \(B_{c1}\) is obtained from their Gibbs-energy difference. The calculation resolves the vortex core and its finite-width deformation without introducing a cutoff. The resulting vortex self-energy is larger than the naive Pearl--London estimate and cannot, in general, be represented by a London logarithm with a single width-independent cutoff. The formulation applies at any \(T<T_c\) and provides a microscopic basis for predicting \(B_{c1}\) in superconducting nanostrips and related thin-film devices.
summary: This paper provides a microscopic theory for calculating the lower critical magnetic field (B_c1) in superconducting thin films by solving the 2D Usadel equations. It overcomes limitations of older models by self-consistently resolving the vortex core structure, demonstrating that the resulting energy scale differs significantly from simple London predictions. This work establishes a robust theoretical basis for predicting superconducting behavior in nanoscale devices across various temperatures.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop a microscopic theory for determining the lower critical field (B_c1) in superconducting thin-film strips, addressing shortcomings in standard phenomenological models.
main_result: The microscopic calculation resolves the vortex core structure without needing an arbitrary cutoff, showing that the resulting vortex self-energy significantly deviates from naive Pearl-London estimates.
method: The authors solve the two-dimensional Usadel equations self-consistently for both vortex and Meissner states at fixed magnetic fields to calculate B_c1 via Gibbs energy differences.
model_or_system: The system is a narrow superconducting thin-film strip. The theory uses the dirty limit approximation solved via 2D Usadel equations, incorporating the applied magnetic field directly into the momentum terms.
key_observables: Lower critical field (B_c1), dimensionless vortex self-energy factor (E_v), and edge barrier field (B_s).
important_parameters: Dirty-limit coherence length (xi), Pearl length (Lambda), normalized strip width (w = W/xi), and temperature (T < Tc).
main_assumptions: The film is assumed thin enough that superconducting parameters are uniform across the thickness dimension; magnetic screening by the strip itself is neglected.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares self-consistent Usadel results for B_c1 vs. width (w) against the naive Pearl-London estimate. Figure 2 shows the temperature dependence of E_v, comparing Usadel results to empirical fits derived from the theory.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical problem and limitations of existing theories; it then details the microscopic framework using the Usadel equations solved self-consistently for vortex/Meissner states; finally, it presents quantitative comparisons showing the deviation from simple London models across varying temperatures and widths.
why_interesting: While focused on superconductivity, the rigorous application of advanced continuum field theories (Usadel equations) to resolve fundamental physical quantities like core structure without ad-hoc cutoffs is a valuable methodological contribution applicable to other strongly coupled quantum systems where approximations are common.
